name: a-frost-park-from-above
prompt: A tall vertical drawing, pure black ink on cream newsprint, looking steeply down from a high vantage onto a small city park on a frozen January morning in 1919. The whole top third is open winter sky, pale and blank, untouched by the pen. Below it the park unfolds in exact two-point perspective: a curving gravel path dusted with hoarfrost, a row of leafless elms whose every twig is drawn as a fine forking line, a spiked iron railing receding toward the corner, one fluted gas lamp standing beside the path. Shadows and the dark bark are built from patient layered hatching, three and four directions deep, the frosted grass left as stippled white. Small in the lower third, seen from above, sits a single slatted wooden bench. A stout, bulging gentleman in a silk top hat and fur-collared overcoat sits bolt upright and spreads across most of its length, one gloved hand lifted, palm flat outward, brushing someone away. Squeezed onto the bench's last foot of seat, a thin young ex-soldier in a worn army greatcoat bends toward him, one trouser leg folded and pinned below the knee, a wooden crutch lying across his lap. A little cloud of breath hangs before each mouth, outlined in a few curling strokes. Cold flat morning light, no colour at all, the drawing reading like a careful plate from a period weekly. The image is drawing only, with no lettering, captions, numbers, or initials anywhere.

name: a-crayon-dismissing-hand
prompt: Upright magazine plate from 1919 rendered entirely in broad black grease crayon rubbed over thin grey ink washes on toothy, ridged board, so the darks crumble into a granular salt-and-pepper grain and every edge is soft, thumb-smudged and velvety, the feel of a lithograph rather than a pen line. The viewpoint is low and very near: filling the bottom of the picture, crisp and enormous, a fat kid-gloved hand with a starched cuff and a gold stud flicks the air outward, fingers fanned in a lazy brush-off frozen at its height. Tucked just behind it and still sharp, a portly magnate seen in profile, heavy jowls folding over a stiff collar, a clipped moustache, drowsy hooded eyes looking nowhere, a stovepipe hat polished to a shine, his elbow propped on the curled cast-iron arm of a park seat. Deeper in the picture, blurred and rubbed soft as though the crayon was wiped with a finger, a hollow-cheeked young private in a creased khaki tunic grips a wooden crutch, one leg ending at the knee with the trouser folded and pinned, his gaze locked on that waving hand. Late dusk: a lone gas lamp beyond the right edge rakes long slanted crayon shadows across the scene and catches a thin pale edge of bare paper on the hat brim and the knuckles. The top third of the image is an almost empty field of deep soot-grey evening tone with a few faint scratched twigs, quiet room for words to be laid over later. Colours limited to black, graphite grey and warm cream paper; the board stays free of any written word, numeral or mark of authorship. Thanks.

name: a-behind-the-bench-noon
prompt: Upright newspaper cartoon from about 1919, inked quickly with a steel nib on smooth board and run off on cheap pulp stock that has browned to the colour of weak tea, with slight grain and a ghost of the reverse page bleeding through. The viewpoint is a few steps behind a slatted park bench at standing height, so both sitters face away from us. Right half of the seat: a colossal plutocrat shown only from the back, a black frock coat strained across shoulders broad as a sideboard, fat creasing over a stiff white collar, a gleaming stovepipe hat pushed back on his skull; his face is turned a fraction further away from his neighbour while one plump gloved hand swings out to the side at arm's length in an idle, can't-be-bothered brush-off. Left half: a slight young infantryman in a rumpled khaki tunic and peaked cap, back curved, chin dropped to his chest; a wooden crutch rests slanted against the slats by his hip, and under the seat a single hobnailed boot stands on the gravel where two should be, the empty trouser leg folded and pinned. Lines are swift, sure and mostly unbroken outline, with just a handful of hatch strokes in the coat creases and the bench boards. The sun sits straight overhead at midday, so each body drops a tight, solid black puddle directly beneath it and the rest of the scene stays almost unshaded. Behind the bench a bright gravel promenade runs off with promenaders in flat straw boaters, ladies under parasols and clipped plane trees, all touched in with faint, thin, scattered strokes so the two backs dominate. The bottom fifth is open, bare pale gravel, kept empty so words can be set there afterwards. Only black ink on warm browned cream. Nothing written, no balloons, no captions, no labels, no monogram drawn anywhere. Thanks.

name: b-flat-colour-hospital-night
prompt: Tall portrait poster image, styled after a turn-of-the-century German comic weekly printed by colour lithography: confident black brush contours of even weight, each shape filled with one flat, unmodulated ink, and only four inks used in total: black, sodium-lamp orange, clinical teal and an off-white like old newsprint. No tonal blends, no soft shading, no texture fills. The top band of the frame, roughly a fifth of its height, is pure flat black night with nothing in it, kept clear for a caption added later. Underneath, a straight-on eye-level view of a wooden park bench with curly iron arms on a paved forecourt outside a modern hospital at night: the automatic entrance doors read as a glowing off-white block, a flat canopy overhangs them, and the façade is a grid of teal cladding. Overhead on the right, a lamp on a tall post throws a sharp wedge of orange light over the bench, and the shadow beneath the seat is a single crisp black shape. Sprawled across two thirds of the seat, a portly tycoon dressed as in 1910, a tall black stovepipe hat, a long dark frock coat, a pale waistcoat strung with a gold watch chain, knees wide, belly pushed out, a self-satisfied round face; his near arm is stretched out sideways, hand open and palm towards the woman beside him in a dismissive wave. Squeezed onto the far end, a present-day nurse in teal scrubs and grubby white trainers, an ID lanyard round her neck, strands of hair slipping from a claw clip at the end of a night shift, cups a small paper vending-machine coffee in both hands and gazes straight ahead, worn out, paying his hand no attention. Exaggerated cartoon proportions for the two people, crisp simple geometry for the building, a fresh composition of our own. The picture carries no writing at all: no words, numbers, signs or signatures. Thanks.

name: b-two-eras-two-pens
prompt: Vertical drawing, eye-level medium two-shot of one weathered slatted bench at a present-day bus stop on a drizzly grey afternoon, two different hands of ink meeting in a single picture. He occupies the right side: a portly elderly plutocrat in a towering stovepipe hat, swallow-tailed coat buttoned tight over a round belly, gold fob chain, white spats, fat cigar pinched in jewelled fingers. He alone is drawn the old way, built from heavy hatched and cross-hatched strokes in warm brown-black on a slightly foxed, cream-coloured scrap of paper with a ragged scissor edge, so he reads as a figure cut from a hundred-year-old broadsheet and glued onto the page. Nose raised, eyelids lowered, staring off past the frame, he flaps the back of one gloved hand at her in a bored shooing gesture without sparing her a glance. On the left a worn-out nurse in her thirties, teal-blue scrubs beneath an unzipped NHS-style waterproof, ID badge on a lanyard, mobile screen lit in her palm, leans toward him mid-sentence with heavy eyes. She and the whole modern world around her — the glass shelter, kerbstones, puddles reflecting streetlight, a smeared red double-decker sliding past — are drawn in fine, steady, uniform contemporary pen line with gentle cool-grey watercolour washes and no hatching. Thin slanting rain lines fall over everything and bead on the slats. The top quarter of the frame is a plain, pale, washed-out grey sky left completely empty so words can be laid over it later. Palette: warm sepia-black for the gentleman only; cool greys, white paper and a single muted teal for her. Nothing written or printed anywhere in the picture. Thanks.

name: b-over-the-nurse-shoulder
prompt: Vertical editorial cartoon drawn with a dip pen and India ink on cream bristol board, in the spirit of a weekly humour magazine from about 1915 but our own scene: confident tapering contour lines, cross-hatching for the darks, a pencil sketch faintly visible under the ink, and a thin cold wash of blue-grey and gunmetal brushed over it. We look past a nurse who sits on a park bench with her back to us: along the lowest part of the picture, her shoulder in plain hospital scrubs and the knot of her tied-back hair are sketched in a few loose, broken, unfinished strokes, like a near object out of focus. Sharp and large in the centre is the portly rich man beside her, turned toward her and toward us: a gleaming silk top hat, wing collar biting into a heavy jowl, a buttoned waistcoat stretched over his belly. He is mid-brush-off, eyelids drooping half closed with lazy contempt, a thick cigar parked at the side of his mouth, one gloved hand lifted with the palm turned up toward her, done with the conversation. It is just after sunrise and she has worked all night: a pale, low sun sits behind him so a thin line of untouched white paper traces the crown and brim of his hat and the curve of his shoulders, while his face falls into fine hatched shadow. Far behind the bench a modern skyline of glass office towers is suggested in faint hairlines, small and unimportant. The top quarter of the sheet is open, unwashed morning sky for a caption to sit on later. No lettering, speech balloons, signature or numbers drawn anywhere. Thanks.

name: c-banknote-engraving-portrait
prompt: Portrait-format page of warm ivory banknote stock, its upper third and lower third left completely bare, and between them a smooth unadorned ellipse containing a made-up gentleman engraved in the manner of an antique intaglio bill, one ink only, a dark bottle green so deep it reads almost black. He faces us dead centre, cropped just below the chest: a tall glossy silk topper, a broad well-fed face with a double chin spilling onto a starched high collar, a neat waxed moustache, narrow self-satisfied eyes meeting ours and a faint smug curl at the lips. One stubby gloveless hand is raised to his middle, thumb and finger pinching a heavy watch chain draped across a silk waistcoat, a dark tailcoat over it. The whole likeness is made of steady burin grooves: contour lines that swell and taper as they follow the roundness of cheek and forehead, a second set crossing them in the shadow beneath the brim and under the jaw, stippled dots and short dashes softening into bare paper on the highlights of nose and brow, long close-ruled strokes giving the hat its shine, near-solid crosshatch for the coat. Behind him, inside the ellipse, a quiet tint of fine horizontal rules that thins away toward the rim. No guilloche, no scrollwork, no lettering, no numerals, no seal, no serial, nothing written. Lighting is frontal and nearly shadowless, every feature crisp and legible like a character model sheet. A faint wipe of plate tone around the ellipse and the shallow pressed dent of the printing plate in the paper. Thanks.

name: c-split-century-bench
prompt: A tall vertical sheet of old printed cartoon paper torn horizontally across its middle, the two pieces nudged back together so a ragged, fibrous rip zigzags from edge to edge, and through that rip shows a finger-wide strip of pale cream card, empty, reserved for a caption. Top piece, the year 1919: a wooden-slatted park bench with scrolled iron ends, inked in faded brown with a fine steel nib on grainy biscuit-toned stock; behind it a gravel walk, a low spiked railing, a gas lamp on a ribbed column, a bare elm, and far off a tiny lad pedalling a delivery bicycle. Nobody else on the bench; at its right-hand end slumps a portly tycoon, smooth-shaven, heavy jowls, a little pointed moustache, a polished silk top hat tipped forward over his right brow, a double-breasted frock coat tight across the belly, gold fob chain looped over the waistcoat, pale spats, a gloved hand capping a silver-headed walking stick stood between his knees, the other thumb tucked into a waistcoat pocket, eyes drooping with lazy self-satisfaction. Bottom piece, now: that exact bench from that exact viewpoint, inked by the same hand in sharp jet black on whiter stock, but its surroundings updated: a battered council bin, a thin modern street light with a flat LED head, square paving blocks, and a commuter in a hooded parka hurrying by, his face lit cold by the phone he stares at. On the right-hand end the tycoon sits again, an exact twin of the man above: jowls, moustache, hat tipped at precisely the same tilt, tight coat, fob chain, spats, stick, tucked thumb, drooping smug eyes, not one line older. Straight-on eye-level framing at sitting height, the bench drawn the same width in both pieces so its iron ends line up across the tear. One warm low sun from the left lights both centuries the same way, throwing long hatched shadows to the right; shading made of crosshatch and stipple, springy assured outlines, generous bare paper, the hand of a 1910s satirical magazine draughtsman. Every surface in the picture, sign, bin, phone screen and corner, stays bare of any marks: pure drawing. Thanks.

name: c-alone-at-sunset-wide
prompt: Hand-inked brush drawing with watery washes of warm sepia and slate grey on coarse cream paper, the look of a printed weekly paper's political sketch from just after the First World War, deliberately loose and personal rather than polished. Camera sits almost on the ground, low at the near end of a long gravel walk in a city park, staring along it to one plain wooden bench placed exactly in the middle of the picture, the walk's two edges narrowing toward it like rails. Alone on that bench, square in the centre, sprawls a plump, well-fed financier: a black stovepipe topper, a long dark morning coat buttoned over a round belly, a gold fob chain, white spats, one elbow hooked over the backrest and one ankle resting on a knee, smiling faintly with heavy-lidded eyes, untroubled, in no hurry, plainly expecting company. The planks to his left and to his right are empty. A sinking sun behind the lens throws his silhouette and the bench's into a single long black brushstroke that runs down the gravel toward us and almost reaches the bottom border. A handful of pigeons bob and peck around his gleaming patent-leather shoes, each bird a few quick flicks of the brush. The gravel nearest the lens melts into soft, puddled, out-of-focus wash; he and the bench are crisp, drawn in sure pen strokes with fine hatching shading the coat. Everything above the far treeline, the whole upper half of the tall frame, is a smooth sky wash grading from amber-sepia at the horizon to faint pearl grey at the top, utterly bare, no cloud, bird or branch, an open field reserved for overlay text that will be set in afterwards. Faint pale railings and leafless trunks sit low along the distant horizon. Mood: calm, golden, quietly menacing, an evening that ends with him still sitting there. Negative prompt: any writing, type, initials or markings drawn into the image. Thanks.
